title: The Transformation of the Body
english: For admittedly the bodies of all will come back to life clothed with the grace of incorruption, but not all will be changed (1 Corinthians 15:51). The wicked will remain in the form of dishonor, only so that they may be punished; but the righteous alone will be changed, and, besides the good of incorruption, they will be enriched with the covering of divine glory.

So He Himself, by His own power and a working fitting for God, “will transform the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of His glory” (Philippians 3:21). And what is the body of our lowliness? This body from the earth, held fast by death because of that ancient curse (Genesis 3:17–19), which Christ undid by “becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).
The transformation will not carry us off into some other nature. For we shall be what we are, that is, human beings, but incomparably better: incorruptible and imperishable, and glorified besides.

What the last trumpet that raises the dead is meant to show (1 Corinthians 15:52), the inspired Paul himself will make clear to us when he says (1 Thessalonians 4:16), “For the Lord Himself, with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74, Fragmenta in 1 Cor (Greek). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.
The first words of this section’s Greek, ‘εἰκόνος τοῦ Υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ’, finish Romans 8:29 and are rendered at the end of the previous section.
‘τῆς θείας δόξης … τὴν περιστολήν’ is rendered ‘the covering of divine glory’.
‘κατησχημένον’ is taken as the perfect passive of κατέχω (‘held fast’).
The quotation of 1 Thessalonians 4:16 breaks off at the end of the section and continues in the next.

title: The Voice That Raises the Dead
english: …and with the trumpet of God, will come down from heaven” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). “And the dead will be raised incorruptible” (1 Corinthians 15:52).

So he likens to a trumpet the voice of the archangel and that divine and most awe-inspiring command. And even if it is the archangel who cries out and gives the signal of resurrection to those who lie in the earth, still the voice will be Christ’s. For it is He who raises the dead by His own power, and certainly not the archangel’s voice; for every rational creature is yoked under the Master’s commands.

What true resurrection will there be at all, then, unless we say that the very thing held fast by death will come back to life? Or how shall we say, all but dancing in triumph over corruption, “Death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54; Isaiah 25:8), and what follows? “O death, where is your sting? O Hades, where is your victory?” (1 Corinthians 15:55).

It should be known that the blessed Paul cited the passage before us according to the Hebrew text. The Septuagint does not read this way, for it is written in the Prophets, “Where is your penalty, O death? Where is your sting, O Hades?” (Hosea 13:14).
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74, Fragmenta in 1 Cor (Khazarzar transcription). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.

The section opens inside the quotation of 1 Thessalonians 4:16, whose first half (‘with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel’) ends the previous section. The English therefore begins with an ellipsis.
‘κατησχημένον’ is taken as the perfect passive of κατέχω (‘held fast’), as in the previous section.
‘Hebrew text’ renders ‘τὴν ἑβραίων ἔκδοσιν’; Cyril contrasts Paul’s wording with the Septuagint of Hosea 13:14.

title: Sin, the Law, and the Victory
english: “But the sting of death,” he says, “is sin, and the power of sin is the Law” (1 Corinthians 15:56). For the one who holds the sting of death, that is, Satan (Hebrews 2:14), strikes like a scorpion. And he strikes in no other way than through sin. But the Savior has granted us “to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19).

For the sting of death has been destroyed, since sin has been taken away and no longer has the Law as its power. For the Law condemns those who sin; that is why the inspired Paul says that the Law is the power of sin. But this too has been undone in Christ: for sin will not be master over us, because we are not under the Law but under grace (Romans 6:14); and apart from the Law sin is dead (Romans 7:8).

Who, then, supplies us with all these things? Who is the dispenser of righteousness, the giver of freedom, the spring and cause of every good? We shall learn it from the blessed Paul, who says, “But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57).
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74, Fragmenta in 1 Cor (Khazarzar transcription). Original English from the Greek; no English base used.
This section closes the work: it is the end of the fragments on 1 Corinthians printed in PG 74.

Hebrews 2:14 is an echo, not a quotation: Cyril has ‘the one who holds the sting (κέντρον) of death, that is, Satan’, where Hebrews has ‘the one who holds the power (κράτος) of death, that is, the devil’.
πρύτανις (‘presiding magistrate’) is rendered ‘dispenser’, the usual patristic sense when said of God as the source of a gift.
